title: Two Locks, Neither Moves: Deadlock, and Finding It Without Waiting for the Hang

questions.question: Thread 1 locks A then B. Thread 2 locks B then A. When can this hang?
options: When thread 1 holds A and thread 2 holds B at the same moment, so each waits for the other for ever
Never, since each lock is released eventually
Only if both use the same mutex
Only on a single core
questions.explanation: A cycle of lock orders is needed. Measured with the overlap forced: at least one thread gave up every time. With the same order in both threads none did.

questions.question: The same opposite-order code ran in two threads with 100 microseconds of unrelated work between passes, three runs of 4000 passes. How many deadlocks, and what does that tell you?
options: Exactly one in each run
None, which proves the code is safe
None in all three runs, while other gaps showed hundreds or thousands, so a run that does not deadlock proves nothing
Thousands in each run, so it is easy to find
questions.explanation: With no gap: 129, 3739, 3387. With 100 us: 0, 0, 0. With 1000 us: 0, 3, 16. The same bug appeared and vanished with the timing, which is why testing cannot be relied on to find it.

questions.question: Two threads run one after the other, never overlapping: the first takes level 1 then level 2, the second takes level 2 then level 1. What does the level check report?
options: Nothing, since they never ran together and no deadlock was possible
One violation from the second thread, because the order is the bug whether or not the timing ever lined up
Two violations
A deadlock
questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of orders, and the cycle is visible on one thread. Measured: the first thread was clean and the second was refused, with nothing deadlocked and no timing involved.

questions.question: A thread locks a LevelMutex it already holds. What happens, compared with a plain std::mutex?
options: It throws bad_alloc
It is refused and counted as a violation, where a plain mutex locked twice by one thread is undefined behaviour and in practice a hang
The same: it hangs
It succeeds, since mutexes are recursive
questions.explanation: The same level twice is refused, including the same mutex, because locking what you already hold is a cycle of length one. A refusal takes nothing and so cannot block.

questions.question: Why does the suite poll try_lock against a steady_clock deadline instead of using std::timed_mutex::try_lock_for?
options: Because timed_mutex deadlocks
try_lock_for is slow
try_lock_for is not in C++17

Under both gcc 11's and clang 14's thread sanitizers, a try_lock_for that succeeds is reported as 'unlock of an unlocked mutex': 15 of 15 runs measured, because pthread_mutex_clocklock is not intercepted. The program is correct and the tool cannot see it
questions.explanation: A plain try_lock is seen by both sanitizers: 0 of 30 runs reported. Production timeouts should not move to system_clock to quieten a tool, since that jumps when the clock is adjusted.

questions.question: What does a level on a mutex NOT protect you from?
options: Taking locks in decreasing level order
Two threads taking two of these mutexes in opposite orders
The same mutex locked twice on one thread
A lock order that goes through a callback or a condition variable the check does not know about
questions.explanation: It finds the cycles made of these mutexes, and finds them early. A dependency that runs through something it cannot see is outside it, which is why locks are held briefly and nothing unknown is called while one is held.
